observation: One CLI parses options two different ways depending on which namespace handles them. `agent-loop workflow plan SLOP-1 --by Claude` accepts the space-separated form. `agent-loop board card claim SLOP-1 --by Claude` does not, and instead of a usage error it dies with `PHP Fatal error: Uncaught voku\AgentKanban\Exception\ValidationException: Option --by requires a value using --by=<value>.` and a four-frame stack trace ending in `vendor/bin/agent-loop`. The message inside the trace is a good message; it is just delivered as an unhandled exception. Every `board` subcommand inherits this, so the failure mode is reachable from the first board mutation a user attempts.

evidence.summary: `vendor/bin/agent-loop board card claim SLOP-1 --by "Claude" --move-to-doing` printed an uncaught ValidationException with a stack trace through `voku\AgentLoop\Dispatcher->run()`. The same command with `--by="Claude"` succeeded and moved the card to DOING.

`vendor/bin/agent-loop workflow plan SLOP-1 --by "Claude" ...` with the identical space-separated form was accepted and created Contract revision 1, confirming the inconsistency is between namespaces rather than a documented global convention.

hypothesis: The dispatcher forwards argv into each package's own parser without owning a shared option grammar or a shared error boundary, so both the grammar and the exception handling of the sub-package leak through to the user.
validated_conclusion: A dispatcher that presents several packages as one CLI owns the parts the user experiences as one CLI: one option grammar, and one place where a ValidationException becomes an exit code and a one-line message. A stack trace as a usage error is the clearest possible signal that an error path was never walked.
